Wrong. Not wrong in a way that matters much, since the money is already back in your account and the owner has had his week. But wrong, because the form says the speaker was damaged when it arrived, and it wasn't. You dropped it on your first evening, and the shop had no part in that.

Think about who this touches. You got your money back, which is fair if the speaker is no good to you. The owner lost what he was counting on for the week, and you already know that. Further out, there are other buyers and other shops. Every time someone ticks that box when it isn't true, the shop has to charge a little more to cover the false claims, and the people who pay are the next customers. One thing would change my answer. If the shop's own policy says that a damaged item gets a full refund whoever caused the damage, then ticking the box told them something they already agreed to. It still isn't true, but the cost falls on a choice they made. I'd still say the form should say what happened.

Not wrong, as far as you can tell from where you sit.

She dropped it, it stopped working, and she marked that it had arrived damaged. Those two things may not match. A speaker that dies after one evening of being dropped usually means it was dropped. But a form like that is the shop's way of saying what went wrong, and from in there she can only report what she knows of her own evening. She may well believe it arrived damaged, or she may only know that it died on day one. Either way, ticking the box was her way of telling you.

What would make it wrong is if she knew it had arrived fine, dropped it, and wanted a refund without paying for it. Then she would be putting a false picture in your head, and the money would be the cost of that lie. You would be the one paying for it, and so would the next customer, since you would have to charge more to cover the refunds like this one. But you have no sign of that. You have a box ticked and a story about a drop.

So ask yourself what you would do if you were in her place. You would want a fair hearing, and you would want to be believed when you told the truth. She got that hearing when you refunded her without asking. That was good for her, and it cost you your week's profit.

If you want to know more, ask her directly whether the speaker was working when it arrived. She may tell you something you have not heard yet.

And since you are running this alone, you might put a line on the form itself. Ask her to confirm that the item was working when it arrived, and that she is reporting it damaged. Then the next time a box gets ticked, you will know what she meant.

Your loss is real. That is your week's profit, and it is gone. But you have not been cheated, as far as you can tell.

In most places a man may cut back branches that hang over his neighbour's boundary, because they are on his ground, and he does not need your leave to do what is on his own side of the line. Look at what he actually did. He cut the branches that were shading his vegetables, which was his right. He cut them exactly to the line, which shows he was careful about where the cut fell. One thing would change my answer. If the cut went deep into the trunk or around the whole circumference, it could kill the tree, and then the act is much more serious. You say the tree is healthy, so I am going on that. If you see signs of trouble later, look at it again.

You might also ask yourself what you want. The tree is yours, and the fruit is yours. If you want him to ask next time, tell him so. If you want the branches cut, he has shown he is willing to do it.
